5660               	;
5661               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5662               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5663               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5664               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5665               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5666               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5667               	; 	'
5668               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5669               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5670               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5671               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5672               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5673               	; 	'
5674               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5675               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5676               	; 	' above it at all.
5677               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5678               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5679               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5680               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5681               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's
5682               	; 	' beams started falling three pixels short.
5683               	; 	'
5684               	; 	' So the roof gets its own version of the stamp. A beam HOLDS THE ROOF

6471               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6472               	; 			'
6473               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6474               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6475               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6476               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6477               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6478               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6479               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6480               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6481               	; 			'
6482               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6483               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6484               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6485               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6486               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6487               	; 			'
6488               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6489               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6490               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6491               	; 			'
6492               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6493               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6494               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6495               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6496               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6497               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.

7442               	; 		' HE IS STANDING ON A STEP, so he moves at the STEP's rate: 2 px
7443               	; 		' across and 1 up PER PASS -- the staircase's own slope, and exactly
7444               	; 		' what one phase of esc_tick moves the pattern by.
7445               	; 		'
7446               	; 		' NOT `fdv`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. Everything else in this loop
7447               	; 		' is paced by the frame delta, and pacing him that way too made him
7448               	; 		' outrun the steps the moment a pass cost more than one frame: his
7449               	; 		' feet started planted on a tread and ended floating above it.
7450               	; 		' Pacing the ANIMATION by fdv instead is worse -- four phases cannot
7451               	; 		' be stepped by 2 or 3 without aliasing, and the staircase runs
7452               	; 		' backwards (see esc_tick). The only arrangement that cannot drift
7453               	; 		' is the one where both are driven by the same fixed step, so the
7454               	; 		' rider is clocked by the pass, like the steps he is standing on.
7455               	; 		'
7456               	; 		' THE FIRST FEW PASSES ARE THE STEP ON. Walking on, his feet are on
7457               	; 		' the floor and the bottom tread is 4 to 7 px above them, so he
7458               	; 		' climbs at 2 px a pass until he catches it (the tread is rising at
7459               	; 		' 1, so the gap closes at 1 a pass) and then rides with it. Jumping
7460               	; 		' on he lands ON a tread, so eson is 0 and this never runs.

8925               	;
8926               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8927               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8928               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8929               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8930               	; 	'
8931               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8932               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8933               	; 	'
8934               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8935               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8936               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8937               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8938               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8939               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8940               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8941               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8942               	; 	' merged object.
8943               	; 	'
8944               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8945               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8946               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8947               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8948               	; 	'
8949               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8950               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8951               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8952               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8953               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8954               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8955               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8956               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8957               	; 	'
8958               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8959               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8960               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8961               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8962               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8963               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8964               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8965               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8966               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8967               	; 	'
8968               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8969               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8970               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8971               	; 	#if NES
8972               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8973               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8974               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8975               	; 	'
8976               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8977               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8978               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8979               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8980               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8981               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8982               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
8983               	; 	'
8984               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
8985               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
8986               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
8987               	; 	'
8988               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
8989               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
8990               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
8991               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
8992               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
8993               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
8994               	; 	'                   the whole time.
8995               	; 	'
8996               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
8997               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
8998               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
8999               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
9000               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
9001               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
9002               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
9003               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
9004               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
9005               	; 	'
9006               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
9007               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
9008               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
9009               	; 	' they only need setting once.
9010               	; 	'
9011               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
9012               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
9013               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
9014               	; 	' as him changing pose.
9015               	; nes_swp16:
9016               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
9017               	; 	'
9018               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
9019               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
9020               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
9021               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
9022               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
9023               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
9024               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
9025               	; 	'
9026               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
9027               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
9028               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
9029               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
9030               	; 	'
9031               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
9032               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
9033               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
9034               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
9035               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
9036               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0

9038               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0

9068               	; nes_def:
9069               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
9070               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
9071               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
9072               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
9073               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
9074               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
9075               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
9076               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup

9080               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
9081               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
9082               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9083               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
9084               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.

9089               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
9090               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9091               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9092               	; 	'
9093               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9094               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.

9191               	;
9192               	; 	' A PILLAR'S CAP MAY BE CLEARED; AN END WALL'S MAY NOT. beam_one stamps
9193               	; 	' both into the slab row of the band above, but they mean different
9194               	; 	' things. SLABP is the top of a free-standing pillar: a radio or a prize
9195               	; 	' stands in front of the pillar, so leaving its cap up there hangs a grey
9196               	; 	' stub over the fixture and that is what this routine exists to remove.
9197               	; 	' SLABE and ROOFSE are written ONLY at column 0 and column 31 -- read
9198               	; 	' beam_one, they are the two edge cases -- and there they are the
9199               	; 	' BUILDING'S OUTSIDE WALL, carrying its brick bond up through the floor
9200               	; 	' above. Clearing those took the support out from under the storey above
9201               	; 	' at the very edge of the screen, so the second floor visibly rested on
9202               	; 	' nothing.
9203               	; 	'
9204               	; 	' It could only ever show on the ESCALATOR screens, which is exactly how
9205               	; 	' it was reported -- one side, then mirrored on the other. The flight
9206               	; 	' fills the middle of an escalator band, so that screen's radio or prize
9207               	; 	' is pushed right out against the end wall; on every other screen no
9208               	; 	' fixture sits close enough for the two-cell clear at #bca and #bca+1 to
9209               	; 	' reach column 0 or 31.
9210               	; beam_clear:
9211               cvb_BEAM_CLEAR
9212               	; 	' A BEAM TOP IS NOT IN THE TEMPLATE. beam_one VPOKEs it into the row
9213               	; 	' ABOVE each band, out of the pillar-column table -- so on the NES this
9214               	; 	' asks that same table rather than the PPU, and #bca sits one row above
9215               	; 	' the band, which is why it cannot go through nes_tpl.
9216               	; 	'
9217               	; 	' IT ALSO REPRODUCES beam_one'S EXCLUSION OF COLUMNS 0 AND 31. Those
9218               	; 	' carry SLABE/ROOFSE, the building's OUTSIDE WALL, not a pillar cap --
9219               	; 	' and clearing structure because an erase routine could not tell the
9220               	; 	' two apart is the fault that once deleted the second floor's support.
9221               	; 	#if NES
9222               	; 	#nbc = #bca - 8288
9223               	; 	#nbc = #nbc + 32
9224               	; 	#nbc = #nbc - #bdst(nbl)
9225               	; 	nbcol = #nbc
9226               	; 	bcv = 0
9227               	; 	nbi = lv8(nbl)
9228               	; 	nbi = nbi + klsc
9229               	; 	#nbb = #stix + nbi
9230               	; 	#nbp = #stpl + PEEK(#nbb) * 4.
9231               	; 	FOR nbj = 0 TO 3
9232               	; 		nbt = PEEK(#nbp)
9233               	; 		#nbp = #nbp + 1
9234               	; 		IF nbt > 0 THEN
9235               	; 			nbt = nbt - 1
9236               	; 			IF nbt = nbcol THEN
9237               	; 				IF nbt > 0 THEN
9238               	; 					IF nbt < 31 THEN
9239               	; 						bcv = CH_SLABP

10180               	;
10181               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10182               	; 	'
10183               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10184               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10185               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10186               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10187               	; 	'
10188               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10189               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10190               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10191               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10192               	; 	'
10193               	; 	' Three drains support up to 192/64 units per frame. The remainder
10194               	; 	' is below 64, so the byte addition cannot exceed 255. Planes use
10195               	; 	' two-pixel units and double the result outside this shared routine.
10196               	; 	' Other actors retain pixel units and their existing movement rates.
10197               	; 	'
10198               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10199               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10200               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10201               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10202               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10203               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10708               	;
10709               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10710               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10711               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10712               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10713               	; 	' runs every pass.
10714               	; 	'
10715               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10716               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10717               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10718               	; 	'
10719               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10720               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10721               	; 	'
10722               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10723               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10724               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10725               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10726               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10727               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10728               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10729               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10730               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10731               	; 	'

10734               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10735               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10736               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10737               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no

10840               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10841               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10842               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10843               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10844               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10845               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10846               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10847               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10848               	; 	'
10849               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10850               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10851               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10852               	; 	'
10853               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10854               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10855               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10856               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10857               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10858               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10859               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10860               	; 	'
10861               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10862               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10863               	; 	'
10864               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10865               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10866               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10867               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10868               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10869               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10870               	; 	'
10871               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10872               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10873               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10874               	; 	' before any of this.
10875               	; 	'
10876               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10877               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10878               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10879               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10880               	; 	' journey.
10881               	; 	'
10882               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10883               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10884               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.

11345               	;
11346               	; 	' ======================================================================
11347               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11348               	; 	' ======================================================================
11349               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11350               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11351               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11352               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11353               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11354               	; 	'
11355               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11356               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11357               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11358               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11359               	; 	' broken.
11360               	; 	'
11361               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11362               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11363               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11364               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11365               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11366               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11367               	; 	'
11368               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11369               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11370               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11371               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11372               	; coll_obst:

11847               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11848               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11849               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11850               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11851               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11852               	; 	' away from.

12161               	; 	' RIDING WITH THE DOORS SHUT: HIDE HIM AND DO NOT DRAW HIM AT ALL.
12162               	; 	'
12163               	; 	' This test used to sit AFTER his sprites had been written, so every pass
12164               	; 	' placed him at his old floor and then hid him again. That is not free.
12165               	; 	' CVBasic's SPRITE writes a RAM mirror which the vblank ISR copies to
12166               	; 	' VRAM, so a vblank landing BETWEEN the draw and the hide latches the
12167               	; 	' visible state for a frame -- and draw_actors is long (Kelly, Harry,
12168               	; 	' eight obstacles) while a pass on the lift screen spans two or three
12169               	; 	' frames, so it happened constantly. He flickered at the floor he had
12170               	; 	' just left, which reads as a drawing bug rather than as a journey.
12171               	; 	'
12172               	; 	' Deciding BEFORE drawing costs one test and cannot race the ISR at all:
12173               	; 	' the mirror never holds a position to be caught with.
12174               	; 	IF klst = ST_ELEV THEN
12175 DF1C D020  34 	movb @cvb_KLST,r0
     DF1E 21BA

13238               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13239               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
13240               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
13241               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13242               	; 	'
13243               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
13244               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13245               	; 	'
13246               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13247               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13248               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13249               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13250               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13251               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13252               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13253               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13254               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13255               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13256               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.
13257               	; esc_tick:
13258               cvb_ESC_TICK
13259               	; 	' ONLY SCREENS 0 AND 7 CARRY A FLIGHT, so six screens in eight skip this
13260               	; 	' entirely -- which is what makes rewriting the cells every frame
13261               	; 	' affordable. Nested, not `klsc > 0 AND klsc < 7`: the 9900 backend
13262               	; 	' miscompiles a compare-AND-compare (CLAUDE.md 3A).

13282               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13283               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13284               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13285               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13286               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13287               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13288               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13289               	; 	'
13290               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13291               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13292               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13293               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13294               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13295               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13296               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.
13297               	; 	escp = escp + 1

13311               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13312               	; 	'
13313               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13314               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13315               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13316               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13317               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13318               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13319               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13320               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13321               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13322               	; 	'
13323               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13324               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13325               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13326               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13327               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13328               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13329               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13330               	; 	'
13331               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13332               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13333               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13334               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13335               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13336               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13337               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13338               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13339               	; 	' with room to spare.
13340               	; 	'
13341               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13342               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13343               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13344               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13345               	; 	WAIT
13346               	; 	#endif
13347               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13348               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13349               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13350               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13351               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13352               	; 	'
13353               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13354               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13355               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13356               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13357               	; 	'
13358               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13359               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13360               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13361               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13362               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13363               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13364               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13365               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13366               	; 	'
13367               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never
13368               	; 	' move at all.

13987               	; 	' fbase = the top pixel row of level fl's FOUR px band, without a
13988               	; 	' multiply. Four levels at four rows is 16 of the canvas's 24 pixel
13989               	; 	' rows, and the other eight are deliberately empty -- four above and
13990               	; 	' four below -- so the instrument sits in the black with air around it
13991               	; 	' instead of butting against the shop floor above and the screen edge
13992               	; 	' below. The +4 is that top margin.
13993               	; scan_base:
13994               cvb_SCAN_BASE
13995               	; 	' A LEVEL BAND IS SIX PIXEL ROWS ON THE NES AND FOUR ON THE TI.
13996               	; 	'
13997               	; 	' It was six everywhere once. It shrank to four to buy eight empty pixel
13998               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
13999               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
14000               	; 	'
14001               	; 	' On the NES that margin now comes from somewhere else: the name table is
14002               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
14003               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
14004               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,
14005               	; 	' and the instrument goes from 16 pixels tall to 24 -- half again, which is
14006               	; 	' what "not quite so vertically thin" asks for.
14007               	; 	'
14008               	; 	' The TI cannot follow: its name table ENDS at row 23, the scanner is on

14169               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
14170               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
14171               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
14172               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
14173               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
14174               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).

14176               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
14177               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
14178               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
14179               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
14180               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
14181               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
14182               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
14183               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
14184               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
14185               	; 	'
14186               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
14187               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
14188               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
14189               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
14190               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
14191               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick

14194               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
14195               	; 	'

14198               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot

14862               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14863               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
14864               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,

14870               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14871               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14872               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14873               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14874               	; 	'
14875               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14876               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14877               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14878               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
14879               	; 	'

14881               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
14882               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.

15401               	;
15402               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15403               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15404               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15405               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15406               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15407               	; 	'
15408               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15409               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15410               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15411               	; 	'
15412               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15413               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15414               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15415               	; 	'
15416               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15417               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15418               	; 	'
15419               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15420               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15421               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15422               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15423               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15424               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15425               	; 	'
15426               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15427               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15428               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15429               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15430               	; 	'
15431               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15432               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15433               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15434               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
15435               	; bonus_count:
15436               cvb_BONUS_COUNT

15491               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS TALLY B -- a blip that COUNTS rather than a buzz that
15492               	; 	' ratchets. Two frames on and two off at 1,036 Hz (divisor 108), against
15493               	; 	' the 373 Hz it was: the pitch is what separates a count from the
15494               	; 	' timer's own low tick, and the shorter gap makes ten of them a run
15495               	; 	' rather than a queue.
15496               	; 	'
15497               	; 	' NES uses a lower 415 Hz pulse tick (divisor 270); the full catch path
15498               	; 	' in iNES was silent at divisor 108. snd_off has freed channel 1.

15578               	;
15579               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15580               	; 	'
15581               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15582               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15583               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15584               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15585               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15586               	; 	'
15587               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15588               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15589               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15590               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15591               	; 	' counting stops.
15592               	;
15593               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15594               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15595               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15596               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15597               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15598               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15599               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15600               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15601               	; 	'
15602               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15603               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15604               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
15605               	;

15663               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which

15675               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it

15819               	;
15820               	; 	' Silence every channel FIRST. SOUND latches, and the per-channel decay
15821               	; 	' counters are not ticked inside this loop -- a tone still sounding when
15822               	; 	' the pause starts would hang for its whole duration, which is the classic
15823               	; 	' CVBasic sticky-audio failure.
15824               	; 	' EVERY CHANNEL OFF, AND THE DECAY COUNTERS WITH THEM. The counters are
15825               	; 	' ticked by the main loop, so anything still sounding when the loop stops
15826               	; 	' -- for a capture, a death, the bonus count -- sustains for as long as
15827               	; 	' whatever replaced the loop takes. That is where the long beep over the
15828               	; 	' bonus tally came from: not the tally's own note, which turns itself off
15829               	; 	' after every unit, but a footstep or a hit that was still ringing when
15830               	; 	' Harry was caught.

15832               cvb_SND_OFF
15833               	; 	' EVERY CHANNEL sfx_tick CAN WRITE, AND CHANNEL 3 IS ONE OF THEM. This
15834               	; 	' routine was written when the footstep was a pair of tones on channel 0
15835               	; 	' and it still named only 0, 1 and 2 after the footstep moved to the
15836               	; 	' NOISE channel. So a step ringing when Harry was caught was never turned
15837               	; 	' off: it hissed through the whole bonus tally and did not stop until the
15838               	; 	' next round's first footstep happened to reset it.
15839               	; 	'
15840               	; 	' Zeroing sot does NOT silence it. The counter only emits its note-off on
15841               	; 	' the pass it reaches zero, so setting it to zero by hand skips the very
15842               	; 	' write that would have stopped the sound.

15950               	;
15951               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15952               	; 	'
15953               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15954               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15955               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15956               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15957               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15958               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15959               	; 	'
15960               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15961               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15962               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15963               	; 	'
15964               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15965               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15966               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15967               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15968               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15969               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15970               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15971               	; 	'
15972               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15973               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15974               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15975               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15976               	; 	'
15977               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15978               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15979               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15980               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15981               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15982               	; 	'
15983               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15984               	; 	' did not finish.
15985               	; pause_beat:
15986               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT
15987               	; 	GOSUB snd_pend
15988 F3A2 06A0  32 	bl @jsr

15994               	; 	'

16417               	;
16418               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16419               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16420               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16421               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16422               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16423               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16424               	;
16425               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16426               	; 	'
16427               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16428               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16429               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16430               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16431               	; 	'
16432               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16433               	; 	'
16434               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16435               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16436               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16437               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16438               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16439               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16440               	; 	'
16441               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16442               	; 	'
16443               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16444               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16445               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16446               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16447               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16448               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16449               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16450               	; 	'
16451               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16452               	; 	'
16453               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16454               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16455               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16456               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16457               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16458               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16459               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16460               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16461               	; 	'
16462               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16463               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16464               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16465               	; 	'
16466               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16467               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16468               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16469               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16470               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16471               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16472               	; 	'
16473               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16474               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16475               	; 	'
16476               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16477               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16478               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16479               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16480               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16481               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16482               	; 	'
16483               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16484               	; 	'
16485               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16486               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16487               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
16488               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand

16816               	;
16817               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16818               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16819               	; 	'
16820               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16821               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16822               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16823               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16824               	; 	'
16825               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16826               	; 	'
16827               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16828               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16829               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16830               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16831               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16832               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16833               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16834               	; 	'
16835               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16836               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16837               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16838               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16839               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16840               	; 	'
16841               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16842               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16843               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16844               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16845               	; 	#if TI994A
16846               	; 	BANK 2
16847      0776     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept

17978               	; 	INCLUDE "art.bas"
17979               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
17980               	; 	'
17981               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
17982               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
17983               	; 	' being small sprites.
17984               	; 	'
17985               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
17986               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
17987               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
17988               	; 	'
17989               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
17990               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
17991               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
17992               	;
17993               	; spr_kelly:	' Kelly: RIGHT hat/face/two merged run bodies/two FREE slots/duck hat/face/body, then the same LEFT (+36). The run bodies carry tunic AND legs, so a frame is one sprite, and standing is run frame 1. Patterns 0..68
17994               cvb_SPR_KELLY

19116               	; 	' unreadable.

19225               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
19226               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
19227               	; 	'
19228               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
19229               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
19230               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
19231               	; 	'
19232               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
19233               	; 	' blit is
19234               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
19235               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
19236               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
19237               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
19238               	; 	'
19239               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
19240               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.

19875               	;
19876               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
19877               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
19878               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
19879               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
19880               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
19881               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
19882               	; #if NES
19883               	; nes_sky2c:
19884               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
19885               	; nes_bldlc:
19886               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
19887               	; #endif
19888               	;
19889               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
19890               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
19891               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
19892               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
19893               	; 	'
19894               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
19895               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
19896               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
19897               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).
